A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Compute as Teacher work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, figures, tables and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original inference and training experiments on HealthBench and MATH-500 across three model families, together with ablations and synthesis examples.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds RL baseline comparisons, rubric-conditioning and judge-sensitivity experiments, and synthesis-output analyses.

M1.justification: The default frozen-anchor synthesis, reward formulas and GRPO remain. Algorithm 1 replaces hard-coded synthesis with an interchangeable Aggregate input and moves rubric generation outside the rollout loop, specifying a shared rubric. These are limited changes to the written procedure; the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both versions train and evaluate on HealthBench healthcare conversations and MATH-500 mathematics problems. Added controls and analyses use this retained coverage; proposed extensions to dialogues or agentic trajectories are future work.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds Majority Vote-RL on MATH-500 and min(PPL)-RL on both benchmarks for Llama 3.1 8B. The inference-time comparator set and the physician-rubric, model-as-judge and SFT comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: The principal splits, policy sizes, training budgets, default eight rollouts and benchmark metrics remain unchanged. New controlled experiments vary rubric-generation inputs and training judges. The judge-sensitivity experiment uses a fixed Llama 3 70B evaluator, a separate setting from the main GPT-4o evaluations.

E4.justification: v2 adds rubric-conditioning and judge-sensitivity controls, structural and stylistic trace analyses, and model-specific correctness-when-disagreeing analyses. v1 Figure 7's rollout-count sweep is removed, although its one-versus-eight comparison survives in prose. The question-omission experiment, all-rollouts-wrong example and training-plateau analysis are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v1 reports standard-error bars without significance tests or seed counts. v2 adds Welch's t-tests for main comparisons, t-tests for trace statistics, and seven-seed averaging for Table 1. It also specifies that benchmark error bars are computed across test samples; this does not establish additional training runs.

E6.justification: HealthBench synthesis gains over Single change from 8.4%, 8.3% and 12.5% for Gemma, Qwen and Llama in v1 Figure 6 to 17%, 13% and 21% in v2 Figure 5. New results include RL comparisons, rubric conditioning at 0.38 versus 0.34, judge sensitivity at 0.48 versus 0.54, and trace statistics. These are revised or newly reported outcomes, not established gains from a changed core method.

T1.justification: GRPO mathematics moves to v2 Appendix E, while the reward and SFT objectives remain equivalent. Explicit context conditioning in the standard perplexity formula clarifies the existing scoring description. No substantive new theory, assumptions or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: v2 redefines CaT as an aggregation-agnostic RL framework and prioritizes self-proposed rubrics for non-verifiable domains. It adds the headline claim of ninefold lower test-time compute, changes mathematical-domain superiority claims to competitiveness, and drops rollout-count scaling as a main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets similar-length, fewer-equation synthesis traces as selective reuse of reasoning and adds dependence on judge capability. It removes the discussion of reliance on curated questions and introduces future directions involving learned aggregators and richer rubrics. The diversity-collapse limitation remains.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 newly documents synthesis and rubric-generation call counts and parallelization of n-by-G judge calls. Appendix I explicitly includes context in perplexity scoring. Existing prompts, hardware, hyperparameters, sampling settings and early-stopping instructions are retained.

R1.justification: Selection methods shift from competing alternatives to supported reference estimators, while novelty is repositioned around reference-free rubric RL and amortizing inference-time aggregation. Related work gains a Test-Time Scaling subsection. Chu et al. (2025) is added; Pearson (1901) and Lupidi et al. (2024) are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method and discussion are extensively rewritten around reference estimation and reward derivation. The seven-question/results narrative becomes focused experimental subsections, GRPO moves to an appendix, and the former CaT/CaT-RL terminology becomes synthesis/CaT.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns, and the pipeline diagrams are substantially redrawn and simplified. The inference comparison changes from point plots to grouped bars, other plots are restyled, and v2 adds both tabular transcriptions of existing comparisons and new analysis tables. v1 Figure 7 is removed, with its right-panel findings retained in prose.

improvement.justification: The added RL baselines, targeted controls and statistical reporting address gaps in v1. However, v2 introduces unresolved contradictions in the central teacher comparison: Figure 3/Table 2 give Qwen MATH-500 synthesis 0.81 versus CaT 0.83, while Section 4.2 says CaT is worse and Table 5 reports synthesis 0.86. These discrepancies, alongside removal of the rollout-scaling evidence, leave the net quality effect uncertain despite the useful additions.
